newsitem.title: USA: U.N. agency asks for more bilateral aid to N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agency asks for more bilateral aid to N.Korea.

text.p: The United Nations food aid agency appealed to Western countries on Thursday to give more aid to North Korea to meet a shortfall of up to 800,000 tons of food needed to ease a severe famine.

Catherine Bertini, executive director of the World Food Programme (WFP), told a news conference the entire population of North Korea was threatened by the famine, made worse first by floods and now by a devastating drought.
"The World Food Programme is pleading with donors to make bilateral donations," Bertini said. "There are still millions and millions of people who have no food...The whole country is in famine."

Earlier this month, the WFP launched a new appeal for $46 million to ease the plight of about 2.6 million children under 6 years old who are already suffering from critical malnutrion. Bertini said donor response had been very generous and about 75 percent of this money had been raised.
The $46 million would cover about 130,000 metric tons of food. An appeal for $96 million earlier this year had already been covered by donor governments and organisatons.

Bertini said the WFP estimated there was a shortfall of between 700,000 and 800,000 metric tons of food. The WFP could not distribute this aid as it was already stretched ensuring that current donations reached the hungry. Bilateral donations should be made directly to North Korea to cover the shortfall.
People were so hungry they were harvesting crops early, Bertini said. Crops matured the most in the last few weeks, meaning that the harvest could reap only half as much as usual.

She said starving North Koreans had developed a host of survival mechanisms. They were harvesting seaweed and several factories were being used to bake cakes, which had no nutritional value but filled a person's stomach.
"If they (the cakes) look brown, they are made of tree bark, if they are green they are made of tree leaves," Bertini said.
WPF staff touring the country had seen almost no small animals and it was likely these were eaten long ago.
Bertini said it was unclear how many people had died from starvation, adding that a famine monitoring team would soon be sent to in North Korea to assess the situation.

On Tuesday, president of the Geneva-based aid group Food for the Hungry International, said at least 5 million people in North Korea were suffering from a crisis that was reaching the level of the famines in Somalia and Ethiopia.
Bertini said she saw North Korea's famine as more serious than any others she had encountered.
North Korea, which has long proclaimed a policy of self-reliance, has been forced to plead for foreign aid to keep its population alive.
Bertini said the North Korean government had so far been cooperative. The WFP had an office in the capital and had been given permission to open up regional offices.
She said each shipment of food sent to North Korea was closely monitored by aid officials. Allegations that North Korea was selling off corn had proved to be inaccurate.
Recent warnings about the plight of North Korea coincide with efforts by the two Koreas, the United States and China to reach a peace settlement on the Korean Peninsula.
Next Tuesday, senior officials of the four nations are due to meet in New York to set an agenda and other procedural details of the talks.
South Korea has said large-scale assistance could be discussed during the peace talks.
